Ourselves
our-selvz'
pron. (first person plural reflexive; rendering Greek heautous with first-person reference)
A compound of our and selves. It is the pronoun by which a company speaks of its own action upon itself, and in the epistles it becomes the apostolic word for what preachers must not do — preach themselves — and for what they gladly are: servants for Christ's sake.

Biblical Definition

Ourselves is the first person plural reflexive, and its most weighty use in Scripture is Paul's statement of what preaching is not. “For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake” (2 Corinthians 4:5). The word appears twice in one verse and points in opposite directions: the minister is not the message, and the minister is the servant. Both halves are needed, for a man who will not preach himself may still refuse to serve, and a man eager to serve may still contrive to be admired. The same pronoun marks the apostles' ordering of their labour — “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Acts 6:4) — a deliberate refusal of good work in order to keep the best. It marks the fruit of affliction: God comforts us “that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” (2 Corinthians 1:4), so that consolation received is consolation owed. And it marks apostolic restraint in ambition: “we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure” (2 Corinthians 10:14).

Webster 1828 Definition

The reflexive and emphatic form of we; a company speaking of its own action upon itself. In Scripture it is Paul's word for the minister who must not be his own message, for the apostles giving themselves to prayer and the word, and for comfort received in order to be given away.

expand to see more

OURSELVES, pron. [our and selves.] The reflexive pronoun of the first person plural.

2. It is used when the speakers are also the objects of the action; as, we deceive ourselves.

3. It is used emphatically, to distinguish the speakers from all others; as, we ourselves have heard him.

4. The singular form is myself; the reciprocal sense, one another, is distinct from the reflexive.

5. In Scripture, we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord, 2 Cor. 4; we will give ourselves continually to prayer, Acts 6.

Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 4:5 — "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake."

Acts 6:4 — "But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word."

2 Corinthians 1:4 — "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

2 Corinthians 10:14 — "For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as though we reached not unto you: for we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ:"

Modern Corruption

The pulpit that becomes a platform for the preacher is the standing corruption this pronoun rebukes. The modern minister is encouraged to build a personal brand, tell his own story, and be relatable; Paul's rule is that the man in the pulpit is a servant carrying a message that is not about him.

expand to see more

Personality-driven ministry is not a new sin, but the present machinery for it is new. Conferences, platforms, and the whole apparatus of the celebrity pastorate reward the man who is memorable rather than the man who is faithful, and the sermon full of the preacher's own anecdotes will always be more immediately pleasing than the sermon full of Christ. Paul's formula is exact and it is not anti-personal: he does not say we preach no one, but that we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord. The test is simple and searching — when the congregation goes home, whom do they admire?

The second half of the verse guards against the opposite error, a false modesty that hides from people. And ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake: the minister who refuses to be the message must still make himself available as the servant. Acts 6:4 shows the apostles ordering their own labour on this principle, declining even the good work of serving tables in order to give themselves to prayer and the ministry of the word. That was not aloofness; it was the discipline of a man who knows what he is for. Between self-display and self-protection stands the servant, spent on people and pointing away from himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek heautous serves for all the plural reflexives, the person being supplied by the context; Hebrew uses the reflexive stems and nephesh with plural suffixes; English compounds our with selves.

expand to see more

Greek heautous (G1438) — ourselves, yourselves, or themselves; the person is determined by the verb and the context.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald or preach; the verb governed in 2 Corinthians 4:5 by the negative not ourselves.

Greek doulos (G1401) — a bondservant; the word Paul chooses for what the minister is toward the congregation.

Greek proskartereo (G4342) — to give oneself continually, to persevere in; the apostles' word for prayer and the ministry of the word.

Saxon ure and selfe — the possessive and the intensive compounded into the English reflexive.

Usage

"Of the minister who is not his own message: we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord (2 Corinthians 4:5)."

"Of labour deliberately ordered toward the best work: we will give ourselves continually to prayer (Acts 6:4)."

"Of comfort received in order to be given away: the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God (2 Corinthians 1:4)."
